title: The Ram, the Goat and the Small Horn
sum: The language of the book switches back to Hebrew. Two years after the vision of the four beasts, Daniel sees himself at Susa, by the Ulai canal. A ram with two horns butts in every direction and no animal can stand against it. Then a he-goat with one striking horn sweeps across the earth without touching the ground, smashes the ram, and grows great. At its height the great horn breaks, and four horns take its place. From one of them a small horn grows, huge toward the south, the east and the Beautiful Land. It reaches the army of the sky, throws down stars, ends the regular offering and flings down the sanctuary.

A holy one asks how long this will last, and another answers: 2,300 evenings and mornings, and then the holy place will be set right. Gabriel, named here for the first time in the Bible, explains: the ram is Media and Persia, the goat is Greece, and the small horn is a bold king who will destroy many and be broken without a hand. Daniel is told to close up the vision, and he is left sick and stunned.
readings: Read as Antiochus IV

The critical majority, and many conservative scholars, read the small horn as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164 BC). He attacked Egypt, marched east and took Judea. In December 167 BC an altar to Zeus was built on the temple altar and the regular offerings stopped; in December 164 BC Judas Maccabeus cleansed the temple (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52-54). The 2,300 evenings and mornings are the 1,150 days between.
Read as Rome or the papacy

Jewish readers such as Rashi took the horn as Rome (Titus), and Protestant historicists from the Reformation to the 19th century read the horn as pagan and then papal Rome. The Adventist reading counts the 2,300 'days' as years from 457 BC to 1844.
Read as a type of the end

Jerome, and dispensational writers since, say Antiochus is a pattern of the Antichrist: the vision is fulfilled in part under Antiochus and finally in a future persecutor who is broken 'without a hand'.

views.H: The ram is the Persian empire (Cyrus, 550-530 BC, to Darius III), the goat Alexander's conquest of it (334-331 BC), the four horns the successor kingdoms after 301 BC, and the small horn the Seleucid king Antiochus IV. His southern campaigns against Egypt were in 170-168 BC, the desecration in 167 BC and the rededication in 164 BC, within a year of his death.
views.C: Most critical scholars read chapter 8 as written between the desecration (167 BC) and the rededication (164 BC): it describes Antiochus' acts with great precision but not his death or the cleansing of the temple, only that he will be 'broken without a hand' (8:25). The sixth-century view takes the same events as prediction made over three centuries before; they point to the book's own claim to date from Belshazzar's third year and to the rise of Persia and Greece as events it names ahead of time.
views.J: Jewish readers have seen Greece and Antiochus in the vision (Josephus, Antiquities 12.7.6, says Daniel foretold the desolation under Antiochus), and also Rome: Rashi, read on Sefaria, takes the small horn as the kingdom of Titus.
views.X: The church fathers and Jerome used Antiochus as a type of the Antichrist (Jerome gives Porphyry's reading and the church's side by side). Calvin reads Antiochus. The Adventist church reads the 2,300 days as years ending in 1844 and the sanctuary as the one in heaven (Fundamental Belief 24). Dispensational readers see a double fulfillment.
views.F: Readers who look ahead take the small horn, at least in its final form, as the Antichrist of the last days, and 'the time of the end' (8:17, 19) as the end of the age; the 2,300 days are then a literal span in the future tribulation, or the persecution's total.

deep.b:
For Daniel 8-10 the Plain is translated from the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), verse by verse from a word-for-word rendering. The Dead Sea Scrolls were read in the transcriptions of Martin Abegg, James Bowley and Edward Cook (ETCBC dss), and what each preserves is stated by its visible words; words the editors restore in gaps are never cited as a scroll's reading. 4QDan-a (4Q112) is visible in 8:1-5 and 10:16-19, with only the first two words of 10:20. 4QDan-b (4Q113) is visible in 8:1-8 and 8:13-16 (in 8:14 the hundreds are restored). 6QpapDan (6Q7) is visible at 8:17, 8:20-21 and in parts of 10:8-16 (at 8:16 only one restored word survives). 4QDan-c (4Q114) is visible in 10:5-19 and 10:21, with nothing visible at 10:20. 4QDan-e (4Q116) is visible in 9:12-17, apart from restored words (in 9:13 the transcription places the restored divine name after 'your truth', so the word order there cannot be judged). No scroll preserves 8:9-12, 8:18-19, 8:22-27, 9:1-11, 9:18-27 or 10:1-4, including all of the seventy sevens. The Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints the Old Greek from the Chigi manuscript (Codex Chisianus) and Theodotion separately; the critical Göttingen Daniel and Papyrus 967 were not checked, so 'the Old Greek' here means Chigi as Swete prints it. The medieval Jewish commentaries cited (Rashi on chapters 8-10, Ibn Ezra on 9:24-25, and Seder Olam Rabbah 28) were read in the Sefaria edition. Everything else is cited as reported by the works named in the notes.

The variants list the places where the witnesses differ in meaning: the opening of 8:1, one great ram (8:3), the extra 'east' (8:4), the Greek of 8:9, the active or passive verb (8:11), the number in 8:14, the Ketiv and Qere of 9:12 and 9:24, the Greek of 9:17 and 9:24-27, the year in 10:1, and the hand of 10:16.

deep.h: Why this chapter matters to the book
deep.b: Chapter 8 is the first vision after the Aramaic chapters and the first to be explained by an angel by name. It gives two of the empires of chapters 2 and 7 their names (Persia, Greece), and so is the anchor for every reading of the four kingdoms. It shows the book's central pattern: a vision of great power, a limit on that power ('without a hand', 8:25), and a holy place restored. And it introduces the Greek-period crisis (Antiochus) that chapters 9 and 11 take up.

deep.h: Why a ram and a goat?
deep.b: The angel says what the animals mean, so the text itself settles the identification (8:20-21). Why those animals is a different question. Ancient peoples used animals as emblems, and a prophet could pick a pair that suited the story: the ram, a leader of the flock with strong horns, for a king who butts in every direction; the he-goat for a younger power that moves faster and crushes the ram. Nothing in the text says that Persian or Macedonian symbols lie behind the choice, and the claim is made without proof by some commentators. Compare the beasts of chapter 7, which the angel explains in less detail.

echoes: Daniel 2:31-45; Daniel 7:1-27; Daniel 9:24-27; Daniel 10:20; Daniel 11:2-45; Joshua 5:13-15; Isaiah 14:12-15; 1 Maccabees 1:10-64; 1 Maccabees 4:36-59; 2 Maccabees 9; Revelation 12:4; Revelation 22:10

settings.what: The vision of the ram, the goat and the small horn
settings.by: Daniel, telling what he saw in a vision at Susa
settings.to: Within the story, no one but Daniel; the book's readers are the Jews who would hear it read
settings.when: In the third year of King Belshazzar, about 550 BC on the traditional dating, two years after the vision of chapter 7
settings.why: To show that the two empires over God's people, Persia and Greece, rise and fall within his plan, that a Greek king will attack the temple and the regular offering, and that there is a stated limit ('until when?', 8:13-14) after which the holy place will be set right. The question 'How long?' is the question of anyone living through a persecution.
settings.readers: For Jews reading the book in the 160s BC, the Greek horn is not a puzzle: it is the king who is now stopping the offerings, and the 2,300 evenings and mornings are the count of days they are living through. Later readers (the Septuagint's Jews in Egypt, Qumran, the early church) read it as the pattern of every persecutor.
views: Traditional view: Daniel, an official in Babylon, was shown this vision in the exile and wrote it down for the Jews of Babylon and Persia and for those after them, who would live to see the Greeks and Antiochus fulfill it.
Critical view: a Jewish teacher in Judea during the persecution of 167-164 BC wrote in Daniel's name to tell faithful readers that Antiochus' reign was foreseen and would be short.

settings.by: The angel Gabriel, sent by a voice over the Ulai
settings.to: Daniel, called 'son of man', terrified and on his face
settings.when: Right after the vision, at Susa, before Daniel is raised to his feet
settings.why: To name the kingdoms (Media and Persia, Greece), to describe the final king, to tell Daniel that the vision concerns 'the time of the end', and to say that it is true but to be closed up. It turns a puzzling picture into a history that the hearer can place.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, the explanation is the proof that the animals mean the empires they know; the order ram, goat, four horns, small horn is their own history in a few lines.
views: Traditional view: the closing of the vision (8:26) means it was kept sealed until the days it describes; the book was kept until then.

Critical view: the command to close up the vision is a literary device by which a book written in 165 BC claims to have been written long before; it assures readers that the author did not know the end of the story from the inside.

traditions.q: Daniel 8:14: what are the 2,300 evenings and mornings, and what is the sanctuary that will be set right?
views: The 2,300 'days' are years, counted from 457 BC (the decree of Artaxerxes, Ezra 7) to 1844, when Christ began the last phase of his work in the heavenly sanctuary, the investigative judgment, which shows who among the dead and the living are in Christ (Fundamental Belief 24, 'Christ's Ministry in the Heavenly Sanctuary'). The word 'set right' (nitsdaq) is tied to the Day of Atonement cleansing. Some Adventists, such as Desmond Ford in 1980, questioned parts of the argument.

There is no defined Catholic interpretation. Jerome set out Porphyry's reading (Antiochus) beside the church's (a type of the Antichrist), and many Catholic scholars today, such as Hartman and Di Lella in the Anchor Bible, read the 2,300 evenings and mornings as the period of the temple's desecration under Antiochus IV, ended by the rededication of 164 BC.
Calvin, in his lectures on Daniel, read the little horn of chapter 8 as Antiochus Epiphanes and the cleansed sanctuary as the temple restored under Judas Maccabeus.

Chapter 8 was fulfilled in part under Antiochus IV, but its language of 'the time of the end' also points to the Antichrist of the last days, who will do what Antiochus began; the 2,300 days are a literal span.

title: The Prayer and the Seventy Sevens
sum: In the first year of Darius the Mede, Daniel finds in the scrolls that Jeremiah's seventy years for Jerusalem's ruins are nearly done. He answers with fasting and a long prayer: God is faithful and in the right, the people have sinned and rebelled, the curse in the law of Moses has fallen, and the city that bears God's name lies in ruins. He pleads not for the people's righteousness but for God's compassion and his name.

While he is still praying, Gabriel flies to him at the hour of the evening offering. Seventy sevens have been marked off for his people and city: to end the rebellion, finish sin, atone for guilt, bring in lasting righteousness, seal up vision and prophet, and anoint a most holy place. The sevens are counted from a word to restore Jerusalem: seven sevens, then sixty-two, then one. An anointed one is cut off; a coming ruler's people destroy city and holy place; sacrifice stops; an abomination and a desolator come, until the decreed end falls on him. This is the most argued passage in the Bible.
readings: Read as the Maccabean crisis

Seventy years of Jeremiah become seventy sevens of years, about 490 years from the destruction of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC to 164 BC. The anointed one cut off is Onias III (murdered 171 BC), the last seven is the persecution, the desecration is Antiochus' (1 Maccabees 1:54), and the numbers are schematic (Collins and the critical majority).
Read as Christ and AD 70

The sevens lead to Jesus: the anointed one cut off is Christ, his death ends sacrifice, and the Romans destroy city and temple in AD 70. The count varies: from Artaxerxes' seventh year (457 BC) or twentieth (445/444 BC), or symbolically (Africanus, Eusebius, Jerome, Calvin, Young, Baldwin).
Read with a gap

Sixty-nine sevens run to Christ; a gap (the church age) separates them from the seventieth, which is still to come: seven years in which a coming Antichrist makes a covenant with Israel and breaks it in the middle (Anderson, Scofield, Walvoord).
Read in Jewish tradition

Rashi counts 70 years of exile and 420 of the Second Temple, ending in the destruction of AD 70; the first anointed one is Cyrus and the second Agrippa. Ibn Ezra, on Sefaria, counts the seven sevens to the coming of Nehemiah and the sixty-two as the years of the Second Temple, and disagrees with Saadia Gaon's count of 490 years. Medieval Jewish commentators do not agree with one another. The Talmud discourages calculating the end (Sanhedrin 97b).

views.H: Daniel 9:1 dates the chapter to the first year of Darius the Mede, about 539/538 BC, just before Cyrus's decree (Ezra 1:1-4). Gabriel's count is read against Persian and Hellenistic history: the return and temple (538-516 BC), Ezra and Nehemiah (458 and 445 BC), the rise of Antiochus (175 BC), and the destruction under Titus (AD 70).
views.C: The prayer (9:4-19) differs in style and in its use of the name YHWH from the rest of the book, and may be an earlier liturgical prayer made part of the chapter. The seventy sevens reinterpret Jeremiah's seventy years, a well-known exegetical move, and the arithmetic is not exact: 490 years from 587 BC reach 97 BC. The critical majority thinks the author was writing in the Maccabean crisis and counted schematically.
views.J: Medieval Jewish commentators disagree. Rashi (read on Sefaria) counts 70 years of exile and 420 of the Second Temple, to the destruction of AD 70, with Cyrus as the first anointed one; Ibn Ezra (on Sefaria) counts the seven sevens to Nehemiah and the sixty-two as the Second Temple's years. Seder Olam Rabbah 28 gives 70 years for the destruction and 420 for the Second Temple. The Qumran Melchizedek scroll (11Q13) arranges history in jubilees and uses Daniel 9:25 of an eschatological figure (as reported by its editors).
views.X: From Africanus and Hippolytus onward, most Christian interpreters have seen Christ in 9:24-27. The early church counted the sevens to his coming; the Reformers (Calvin) to his death and the fall of Jerusalem; dispensational writers to his entry into Jerusalem, with a gap before the last seven. Adventists count from 457 BC to AD 27 and 34.
views.F: Futurists take the seventieth seven (9:27) as still to come: a seven-year tribulation, in which the covenant with 'the many' and the halting of sacrifice at the midpoint belong to the Antichrist (Daniel 7:25; Matthew 24:15; 2 Thessalonians 2:4; Revelation 11-13). Critics of the gap, including some premillennialists, say the text gives no hint of a break between the sixty-ninth and seventieth.

deep.b:
Every reading answers the same questions: where the count starts, what a 'seven' is, who the two anointed ones are, who 'he' is in 9:27, whether there is a gap, and what happens to the temple. A short list follows; the topic page on Daniel's Seventy Sevens sets them side by side.

  • Antiochene (critical majority): start 587/586 BC (or Jeremiah's word); 7 sevens (49 years) to Cyrus or Jeshua (538 BC); 62 sevens to Onias III (171 BC); the last seven 171-164 BC, the half-seven 167-164 BC; no gap; the temple is cleansed in 164 BC. The numbers are schematic.
  • Messianic (church fathers, Reformers, Young): the 490 years reach Christ; the anointed one cut off is Christ; the sacrifices end with his death; AD 70 ends the city and sanctuary. Starts from 457 or 445/444 BC, or a symbolic count.
  • Adventist: start 457 BC; 69 sevens to AD 27 (baptism); the half-seven to AD 31 (the cross); the 70 sevens to AD 34; and the 2,300 days (8:14) run on to 1844.
  • Dispensational: start 445/444 BC; 69 sevens of 360-day years (483 years, 173,880 days) to the triumphal entry (AD 32 or 33); a gap; a future seven-year tribulation.
  • Historicist and preterist: the sevens end in the first century; the day-year principle for other numbers; the preterist ties the half-seven to AD 66-70.
  • Jewish (medieval commentators, who disagree): Rashi: 70 years of exile + 420 of the Second Temple; Cyrus; Agrippa; Titus. Ibn Ezra: seven sevens to Nehemiah, sixty-two for the Second Temple.
  • Jehovah's Witnesses: start 455 BC (Nehemiah 2); 69 sevens to AD 29 (Jesus' baptism); the seventieth seven to AD 36.

The two Greek versions differ more here than anywhere else in the chapters. In Swete's printing the Old Greek (Chigi) has seven clauses in 9:24 against the Hebrew's six, and no number of sevens in 9:25. For 9:26 it has 'after seven and seventy and sixty-two' (the word 'sevens' is not there: the Greek reads "seven, seventy and sixty-two"), 'an anointing will be removed', and 'a kingdom of nations will destroy the city and the holy place with the anointed one'; its 9:27 says the covenant will 'rule over many', speaks of 'seventy-seven times and 62 years' and 'many weeks', and ends the sacrifice 'at the end of the week'. Theodotion is close to the Hebrew: 'sixty-two sevens ... an anointing will be destroyed, and there is no judgment in him', and it puts the abomination 'on the temple' (hieron). Jerome's preface to Daniel is the usual witness that the churches read Theodotion's text in place of the Old Greek; Origen's letter to Africanus concerns Susanna, not this passage. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the Greek differences appear in the variants and notes.

The prayer (9:4-19) is a mosaic of older scripture: Solomon's temple prayer (1 Kings 8:46-53), the confessions of Ezra 9 and Nehemiah 9, the law's curses (Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 27-30) and lament psalms (Psalm 79). Its argument has three steps: God keeps his covenant and is in the right (9:4-14); he showed his power at the exodus (9:15); therefore he should forgive for his own name's sake (9:16-19). It is a liturgy of fasting as much as a private confession, and the Baruch of the deuterocanon (Baruch 1:15-3:8) and the Prayer of Azariah in the Greek Daniel adapt it.

echoes: Jeremiah 25:11-12; Jeremiah 29:10; 2 Chronicles 36:21-23; Leviticus 25:1-7; Leviticus 26:34-45; Deuteronomy 28-30; 1 Kings 8:46-53; Ezra 9:6-15; Nehemiah 1:5-11; Nehemiah 9:5-37; Psalm 79; Isaiah 10:23; Isaiah 53:8; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14; Luke 1:19; Luke 21:20-24; Hebrews 9:11-28; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 2 Maccabees 4:33-38; Baruch 1:15-3:8

settings.what: Daniel reads Jeremiah and turns to God
settings.to: The book's readers; within the story, God alone
settings.when: In the first year of Darius the Mede, about 539/538 BC, as the seventy years of Jeremiah near their end
settings.why: To show Daniel acting on a written prophecy by praying, not by waiting: the promise of return is a reason to confess. His fast and sackcloth show he expects an answer.
settings.readers: For readers in exile or under persecution, Daniel is a model of how to read scripture: as a prompt for prayer.
views: Traditional view: Daniel, in Babylon, read Jeremiah's scroll in his own time and prayed for the return that began soon after (Ezra 1:1-4).
Critical view: the author, writing about 165 BC, shows an ideal Daniel reading Jeremiah, to prepare the way for a new reading of the seventy years that fits his own day.

settings.by: Daniel, in the first person plural, 'we'
settings.to: The LORD, 'my God'; overheard by the exiles and the later readers
settings.when: During the three weeks of fasting, as the time of the evening offering approaches (9:21)
settings.why: To confess that the exile is the covenant's curse and is just; to appeal to God's compassion and to his name; and to ask him to restore Jerusalem and the sanctuary. The prayer is the pattern of a public fast day: confession, justification of God, a plea.
settings.readers: For the exiles and later Jews this became a prayer of their own, used at fasts for the temple's destruction; Baruch and the Prayer of Azariah reuse it, and it shaped the liturgy of repentance.
views: Traditional view: Daniel's own prayer in Babylon, spoken for the whole people.

Critical view: an older liturgical prayer, perhaps from the Persian period, fitted to the chapter by the author; or his own work in an established style, for Jews who read the persecution of 167 BC as the curse of the law again.

settings.to: Daniel, 'a highly treasured man', and through him 'your people and your holy city'
settings.when: At the time of the evening offering, as Daniel is still praying
settings.why: To tell Daniel that the time of Jerusalem's ruins is not simply seventy years, that a longer course of seventy sevens has been decreed for his people and city, and that it ends in the ending of sin and the anointing of a most holy place, but only after a ruler comes and destroys, and a desolator is judged.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, the answer meant the long delay after the return was not a failure of Jeremiah's word but part of a longer plan, and that their own sufferings had a decreed end. Christians, Jews and Adventists have each seen their own history in it.
views: Traditional view: spoken to Daniel in 539 BC, looking forward to the second temple, Christ or the end of the age, according to the reader.
Critical view: addressed to Jews under Antiochus IV, in Daniel's name, to say that Jeremiah's seventy years had been renewed as seventy sevens and were now almost complete (164 BC).

traditions.q: Daniel 9:24-27: what are the seventy sevens, and is there a gap before the last seven?
views: The Church has defined no reading. The Fathers (Augustine, City of God 18.34; Jerome, who records several counts) took the sevens to reach Christ. Many modern Catholic scholars, such as Hartman and Di Lella (Anchor Bible), read them of Jewish history to Antiochus IV and the murder of Onias III (171 BC).

No council or catechism defines a count of the seventy sevens. Orthodox churches read the early Fathers, who mostly took the sevens to Christ. Hippolytus of Rome, writing in Greek about AD 200, took the sixty-nine sevens to Christ's coming and the seventieth as a seven-year period still to come at the end of the age, with Antichrist, Elijah and Enoch (On Christ and Antichrist 43, 47, 64); Julius Africanus, as Eusebius reports him, counted the whole 490 years to Christ. No modern Orthodox commentary has been quoted here.
Luther's preface to Daniel treats the chapter's weeks as foretelling the coming of Christ and the fall of Jerusalem, and the count is not a point of Lutheran doctrine.

The sevens end at Christ's death and the destruction of Jerusalem; 'he confirms a covenant with the many' is Christ, who ends sacrifice by his death (Calvin on Daniel 9; E. J. Young). There is no gap.

Sixty-nine sevens of 360-day years run from the decree of 445/444 BC to Christ's entry into Jerusalem. A gap, the church age, separates them from the seventieth, a seven-year tribulation in which the Antichrist makes and breaks a covenant with Israel (Anderson, Scofield, Walvoord).

The 490 years begin in 457 BC, and 69 sevens reach AD 27 (Christ's baptism, 'the anointed one'); he is cut off at the midpoint (AD 31); the seventy end in AD 34. They are cut off from the 2,300 days of 8:14, which end in 1844 (Fundamental Belief 24).

The sixty-nine sevens run from 455 BC (the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, Nehemiah 2) to AD 29, Jesus' baptism and anointing as Messiah; the seventieth seven ends in AD 36 with the first Gentile converts.

title: The Man in Linen and the Princes
sum: In the third year of Cyrus, Daniel mourns for three weeks, eating no fine food, meat or wine and using no oil. On the twenty-fourth day of the first month, standing by the Tigris, he sees a man in linen with a golden belt, a body like chrysolite, a face like lightning, eyes like torches, arms and feet like polished bronze, and a voice like a crowd. Only Daniel sees; his companions run away in terror. He collapses, and a hand stirs him, touches his lips and strengthens him.

The man says Daniel's prayer was heard on the first day, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia held him back for twenty-one days until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help. He has come to tell what will happen to Daniel's people in the last days. Now he must go back to fight the prince of Persia, and the prince of Greece will come; but first he will tell what is written in the writing of truth. No one stands firm with him except Michael, Daniel's prince. The chapter is the doorway to chapter 11.
readings: Read as heavenly war

Behind the empires of the earth stand spiritual powers, the 'princes' of Persia and Greece, and Michael fights for Israel. Earthly events (11:2-45) answer to a struggle above, and prayer and fasting enter it (Daniel 10:12-13).
Read as the setting for chapter 11

The chapter is mostly the introduction to the long survey of the kings of the north and south. The angel's long delay, his fight and his book of truth serve to make the history of chapter 11 feel decreed ahead of time (Collins).
Read as a Christ vision
Some Christian readers take the man in linen to be the preincarnate Christ because his description and Revelation 1:13-16 match; others read an angel, noting that he is sent, delayed and helped.

views.H: The date is about 536 BC: the exiles had begun to return (Ezra 1-2), the temple foundation was soon laid (Ezra 3), and Persia was unsettled by opposition (Ezra 4:1-5). Daniel, near 85, stays. The 'prince of Persia' and 'prince of Greece' look ahead from Cyrus to Alexander.
views.C: Most critical scholars take chapters 10-12 as one unit written in the Maccabean crisis, and chapter 10 as its introduction. The date 'third year of Cyrus' matches the book's last dated vision. The angelic princes show the book's apocalyptic worldview: history is set in a heavenly conflict (compare Deuteronomy 32:8-9 in the Qumran text and the Septuagint).
views.J: Rashi, read on Sefaria, says the prince of Persia asked in heaven for Persia's rule to be lengthened so that it could keep Israel subject. Jewish tradition also makes Michael Israel's advocate (Daniel 12:1; the rabbis speak of him as the guardian angel of Israel). The man in linen is not named by Rashi.
views.X: The early church often saw Christ in the man in linen (because of Revelation 1:13-16), though others take an angel; Michael is the archangel of Jude 9 and Revelation 12:7. Many Christian writers, ancient and modern, have seen demonic powers behind pagan nations here, and modern 'spiritual warfare' teaching draws on 10:13.
views.F: Readers who look ahead take the angelic conflict as continuing until the end of the age: Michael will rise in the time of trouble (12:1), and the prince of Persia and Greece point to powers behind the final world empire in Revelation 12-13.

deep.h: Angels over nations: the idea and its background
deep.b: The belief that each nation has a heavenly patron is old. The Hebrew Bible keeps traces of it: in the Qumran and Greek reading of Deuteronomy 32:8-9, God divides the nations 'to match the number of the sons of God' and keeps Israel as his own share; Psalm 82 has God judging the 'gods' of the nations. Sirach 17:17 and Jubilees 15:31-32 say it plainly, and the Qumran War Scroll gives Michael leadership against Belial. Daniel 10 shows the idea fully developed: princes of Persia and Greece, Michael as Israel's prince, and a struggle in which human prayer matters. Readers differ on whether these princes are loyal angels, evil spirits, or symbols of nations' rulers; Daniel does not call them evil.

deep.h: Three touches and the structure of the chapter
deep.b: The chapter has a clear shape. 10:1-4 is the dating and the preparation; 10:5-9 is the vision and Daniel's collapse; then three touches bring him back, each followed by a speech (10:10-14; 10:15-17; 10:18-21). Compare the sequence of Isaiah 6, Ezekiel 1-3 and Revelation 1, where the prophet falls as dead, is lifted up and commissioned. The long delay of 10:13 is a rare moment in scripture in which the cost of an answer to prayer is explained.

echoes: Genesis 2:14; Deuteronomy 32:8-9; Joshua 5:13-15; Psalm 82; Isaiah 6:1-8; Ezekiel 1:26-28; Ezekiel 9:2-3; Daniel 7:9-10; Daniel 8:15-19; Daniel 9:21-23; Daniel 12:1-7; Acts 9:7; Luke 1:11-20; Jude 9; Revelation 1:12-17; Revelation 12:7-9

settings.what: Daniel's vision of the man in linen
settings.by: Daniel, telling what he saw by the Tigris
settings.to: Within the story, Daniel alone (his companions did not see it); the book's readers
settings.when: On the twenty-fourth day of the first month in the third year of Cyrus, after three weeks of mourning
settings.why: To mark the long revelation of chapters 10-12 as a vision from heaven granted to a man who has fasted and prayed. The terror of Daniel and his companions, and Daniel's collapse, signal that what follows is not a human survey of history but a message from the presence of God.
settings.readers: For readers in the second century BC, a vision by an old man in Persia gave chapter 11's long history a sixth-century voice; for later readers, it set the pattern of the prophet struck down and raised up.
views: Traditional view: a real vision to Daniel in 536 BC, the last of his book.
Critical view: the author's fiction, in the manner of Ezekiel 1-3, to give the final chapters authority.

settings.what: The angel's speech and the princes of Persia and Greece
settings.by: The man in linen, and one who looked like a human being who touched Daniel's lips
settings.when: Right after the vision, as Daniel recovers, still beside the Tigris
settings.why: To assure Daniel that his prayer was heard from the first day, to explain the three-week delay as a struggle with the prince of Persia, to promise that he has come to explain what will happen 'in the last days', and to tell him that the conflict goes on with Persia and Greece and that only Michael stands with him.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, the speech turns the delay of an answer to prayer into a sign of a battle already joined for them in heaven; it is a comfort for people who suffer in a world run by empires.
views: Traditional view: an angel's message to Daniel in 536 BC, preparing for the history of Persia, Greece and the end.
Critical view: the introduction to the Maccabean-era survey of 11:2-12:3, set in Daniel's time so it reads as prediction.

Michael is a created angel, an archangel, the leader of the heavenly host against Satan (Catechism 328-336 on the angels; his feast on 29 September with Gabriel and Raphael). Jude 9 and Revelation 12:7 are read with Daniel 10 and 12.

Michael is the chief of the angels, a created being and the commander of the heavenly host. The Orthodox keep a feast of the Synaxis of the Archangel Michael and the other bodiless powers on 8 November.

No distinct Lutheran statement about who Michael is in Daniel was found in the confessions. Luther's Small Catechism, in its evening prayer, asks God's holy angel to be with the believer, which shows angels as God's servants; no statement about Michael as Christ or as an archangel was found.

Reformed teaching holds that angels are God's created, ministering servants (Calvin, Institutes 1.14), and Reformed commentators are divided about Michael. Calvin, on Daniel 12:1, says that many understand Michael as Christ, the head of the Church, and that if the archangel seems better the sense still fits, since the angels are under Christ's government; on 10:21 he reports that some think Michael to be Christ. He leaves both readings open.

Adventist writing since Uriah Smith has widely taught that Michael is Christ in his heavenly role, citing 1 Thessalonians 4:16 and Jude 9. It is widely held and taught in the church but is not one of the 28 Fundamental Beliefs.
Michael is another name of Jesus Christ: Jesus was Michael before he came to earth and is Michael again as the heavenly king; 'archangel' means chief angel, and Jesus is the chief of the angels.
